subject: Career
title: Writing for Decision-Makers
description: A quick win: understand Writing for Decision-Makers.

hook.text: An executive reads 200 documents a week. If your proposal doesn't communicate value in 30 seconds, it's gone.

buildup.text: Decision-makers need: what's the problem, what do you recommend, what does it cost, what happens if we don't.

discovery.text: Amazon's memo culture works because six-page narratives force clear thinking before meetings.

twist.text: Executives don't want options without recommendations. 'Here are three options' is lazy. 'I recommend option B' is useful.

climax.text: Format for scanning: bold the key points, use bullet lists, and front-load the recommendation.

punchline.text: Write for the person with the least time and the most decisions.

quiz.question: What do decision-makers want from written communication?
options: Problem, recommendation, cost, and consequences — not just options

details.summary: Writing for decision-makers demands extreme conciseness, clear options with trade-offs, and an explicit recommendation. Decision-makers need just enough information to say yes, no, or ask one clarifying question, not a comprehensive education on the topic.
details.whyItMatters: Decision bottlenecks slow entire organizations. Writers who make it easy for leaders to decide quickly accelerate organizational velocity and earn reputational capital.
takeaways: Present two to three options with clear trade-offs for each
State your recommendation and rationale in one paragraph
Attach detailed analysis as an appendix, not the main document

faq.question: What format works best for a decision document?
faq.answer: Use a one-page structure: context in two sentences, the decision needed in one sentence, two to three options with a one-line description and key trade-off for each, your recommended option with rationale, and a deadline for the decision. Attach supporting data separately.

faq.question: How do I handle it when a decision-maker ignores my recommendation?
faq.answer: Accept the decision professionally and execute it fully. Document your original recommendation and rationale privately. If the decision performs poorly, you have evidence of your judgment. If it succeeds, you learn something. Either way, reliable execution maintains trust.
